question: Can abrupt semantic commitments in diffusion sampling be explained as finite-noise competition among nearest-point branches near projection caustics, and does normalized score-direction instability reliably locate intervention-sensitive windows across toy and pretrained generative models?

key_findings.claim: Away from caustics, the paper gives a conventional small-noise Laplace expansion in which one smooth nearest-point branch controls denoising.
key_findings.evidence: For Gaussian smoothing of a smooth data support with a unique nondegenerate projection, the free energy F_sigma=-sigma^2 log p_sigma has leading term one-half squared distance to the support, followed by density and curvature-determinant corrections of order sigma^2 and a uniform O(sigma^4) remainder under the stated regularity. Its gradient therefore approaches the single nearest-branch direction.

key_findings.claim: Main-text Theorem 2.1 overstates the regular regime by treating a unique nearest point as sufficient; the appendix proof silently requires a sufficiently small tubular neighbourhood and a nondegenerate projection Hessian.
key_findings.evidence: The main theorem assumes that the nearest-point projection is uniquely defined and writes a curvature determinant det(I-A_nu), but it does not state positivity or exclusion of focal points. Appendix Theorem B.1 instead fixes a compact set inside a sufficiently small tubular neighbourhood, where the decomposition is unique and I-A_nu stays nondegenerate. A focal point can retain a unique nearest point while det(I-A_nu)=0 and Laplace's quadratic approximation fails, so the main theorem is valid only under the appendix's stronger projection-regular/tubular hypothesis.

key_findings.claim: Near an ordinary nondegenerate projection caustic, the value-level expansion yields a log-sum-exp of competing branches, and the paper claims a corresponding softmax mixture of branchwise score directions.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 2.3 assumes finitely many smooth equal-dimensional nearest-point branches with positive-definite local Hessians and uniform separation from all other support. Summing branchwise Laplace terms rigorously gives the stated local log-sum-exp free-energy value expansion. Corollary 2.4 then states softmax score responsibilities that switch when branch actions differ by O(sigma^2), with density and curvature amplitudes shifting the finite-noise switching locus away from the zero-noise equal-distance caustic.

anchors.section: C Free-energy asymptotics near projection caustics

key_findings.claim: Corollary 2.4's score remainder is not established by the appendix proof: it differentiates a uniform function-value remainder without proving derivative control.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix C proves p_sigma=A_sigma(1+O(sigma^2)) uniformly and therefore F_sigma=-sigma^2 log A_sigma+O(sigma^4) as a value-level statement. Section C.6 then says 'Differentiating (14)' and appends O(1) to the score mixture. Uniform O(sigma^4) control of function values does not imply any bound on the derivative of the remainder; a rapidly oscillating remainder is a standard counterexample. A parameter-uniform C1 Laplace expansion or a direct differentiated-integral argument is required. The leading softmax formula is plausible and may be repairable, but the stated corollary is not proved as written.

anchors.section: C.5 value-level remainder and C.6 differentiation

key_findings.claim: The caustic theorem covers ordinary branch competition, not the full singular geometry likely present in arbitrary learned data distributions.
key_findings.evidence: The local theorem excludes focal degeneracies by requiring uniformly positive-definite branch Hessians, assumes finitely many separated smooth branches of the same dimension, and relies on a smooth support density. The discussion says degenerate Airy- or Pearcey-type regimes require uniform caustic asymptotics. Discrete, stratified, self-intersecting, unequal-dimensional, or learned-score supports are not covered by the proof.

anchors.section: C.8 Scope of the normal form

key_findings.claim: CBD is a practical derivative of normalized score direction, while its finite-difference and trajectory-adapted forms are estimators whose sign, scale, and cost depend on implementation choices.
key_findings.evidence: The ideal Critical Boundary Detector is the Frobenius norm of the Jacobian of u_t(x)=s_t(x)/||s_t(x)||. A Gaussian finite-difference estimator uses extra perturbed denoiser evaluations; TAD probes a central difference along a trajectory-adapted direction. The pseudo-online method divides actual-time TAD by low-noise reevaluation on a fixed baseline state sequence and then normalizes or inverts profiles in later experiments.

key_findings.claim: The pseudo-online label means the diagnostic uses no future sampler modification, but it is not an actually online causal detector.
key_findings.evidence: Algorithm 1 first fixes and stores an entire baseline reverse trajectory, reevaluates every stored state at an artificial low-noise time, forms an actual-to-low-noise ratio, and smooths or normalizes it. A state produced at one noise level need not lie on the model's valid state distribution at another. Thus the signal is available after a baseline rollout plus extra evaluations, not prospectively from the current sampler state alone.

key_findings.claim: The MNIST future-count/prototype experiment is an illustrative qualitative intervention, not a quantitative validation that future-count windows predict semantic commitment.
key_findings.evidence: The method builds one class-conditional baseline trajectory, evaluates each stored state at future reverse times, selects residual-CBD windows using median plus three MAD and additional thresholds, and constructs nearest-prototype repulsion. The 110-200 intervention looks most dramatic, 250-350 and 300-400 look weaker, and 50-75 looks stronger than 85-110. Those judgments are made from displayed images and visually estimated windows; no numerical outcome metric, repeated seeds, class sweep, equal-duration random-window distribution, or blinded semantic rubric is reported. Pages 35-38 are image-dominant qualitative panels and were directly inspected in the PDF.

anchors.section: D.3 Future-count statistic and prototype intervention

key_findings.claim: The cusp toy model supports preferential—but far from exact—alignment between branch commitment and the constructed switching band.
key_findings.evidence: The approximate switching mask occupies about 14.6% of the plotted grid. Across simulated trajectories, 47.1% place their commitment index inside some switching-band residence interval and 52.9% commit outside. Concentration relative to area supports enrichment near the band, but a majority of commitments fall outside and the mask depends on a representative finite noise scale and threshold.

key_findings.claim: On the cross toy distribution, intervening only in the high-CBD band changes branch outcomes substantially, but the intervention is not sparse enough or controlled enough to isolate a minimal causal window.
key_findings.evidence: The vertical-branch fraction rises from 0.5225 without control to 0.9640 with control at every step and 0.8635 with CBD-band control. The band-triggered policy acts for an average 65.5 of 200 steps, roughly one third of the trajectory, and this appendix comparison lacks a matched random band with equal duration and energy. It establishes useful localization relative to always-on control, not unique causal sufficiency of the ridge.

anchors.section: D.2 CBD-guided branch control on the cross dataset

key_findings.claim: CIFAR-10 provides the clearest trajectory-level association between the normalized/inverted TAD profile and downstream intervention sensitivity.
key_findings.evidence: Sliding equal-width perturbation windows along five 250-step baseline trajectories yields per-seed Pearson correlations between the normalized CBD proxy and LPIPS of 0.849-0.966, mean 0.928 with reported p<1e-70. Appendix aggregation of the raw ratio instead reports negative mean Pearson around -0.700 for LPIPS and negative Spearman -0.887, with the inverted 1-R carrying the corresponding positive signs. The magnitude is reproducible, but interpretation requires tracking the inversion.

key_findings.claim: The appendix contains an unreconciled sign and labeling contradiction for the 'TAD ratio': high raw values are alternately said to predict larger effects, while the multi-seed tables say the raw ratio predicts smaller effects.
key_findings.evidence: Page 41 reports Pearson correlations +0.913 with normalized final L2 and +0.919 with LPIPS for a window-averaged 'TAD-ratio.' The same section then says the raw normalized ratio is consistently negatively correlated across five seeds, and Table 3 reports Pearson -0.6939/-0.7005 and Spearman -0.9088/-0.8873, with only 1-R positive. Figure 39 later groups 750 windows each and explicitly says the high 'CBD-ratio' group has substantially larger L2 and LPIPS than the low group. These cannot all use the same raw R convention; the paper never supplies a mapping that resolves whether plotted 'ratio' means R or 1-R, so a deployment policy based on 'high CBD' can be reversed.

anchors.section: D.4 positive TAD-ratio correlations and D.5 sign reversal

key_findings.claim: The classifier-guidance experiment shows that a preselected TAD band can be much more effective than one late random band, but it does not demonstrate per-trajectory online discovery or optimality.
key_findings.evidence: For a pretrained CIFAR-10 DDPM with 250 reverse steps and target class airplane, guidance at ten steps inside fixed t in [30,70] reaches target accuracy 0.960, versus 0.040 for ten steps in the comparison interval [180,220], while full 250-step guidance reaches approximately perfect control. The detector band is fixed from prior analysis and only one random comparison band is used; there is no blinded prospective selection across seeds or matched search over all intervals.

key_findings.claim: Cross-model profile similarity is qualitative and partly induced by per-run normalization, so it does not establish a universal raw critical time or threshold.
key_findings.evidence: The same TAD construction is shown for DiT, EDM2, Stable Diffusion 3.5, face DDPM, and an MDLM caveat, with min-max and trajectory-length normalization used to overlay profiles. Peaks, elbows, and plateaus recur but move with scheduler and model. The paper appropriately says CBD is not a zero-noise caustic estimator or universal order parameter; raw magnitudes and timestep locations are not compared on a common calibrated scale.

key_findings.claim: Stable Diffusion 3.5 exhibits a serious direction-of-effect ambiguity: the raw TAD ratio is negatively, not positively, associated with intervention size in the broad robustness study.
key_findings.evidence: Across 30 prompt-seed runs, mean within-run correlations of window-averaged raw TAD ratio with final effect are Pearson -0.470 for pixel L2 and -0.230 for LPIPS, and Spearman -0.887 and -0.577. Later text and Figure 47 explicitly say windows with small mean TAD yield larger deviations, while other sections call a late interval the 'high-TAD window' and interpret its larger LPIPS as matching TAD ranking. Without a single fixed definition of raw ratio versus inverted 1-TAD, claims that high values mark sensitivity are internally inconsistent.

key_findings.claim: The SD3.5 prompt-switch demonstration is suggestive phase-aware control but is too small to establish a robust semantic-control rule.
key_findings.evidence: The experiment switches prompts at a profile elbow and presents eight generations for one prompt pair/order, arguing that the elbow separates branch selection from refinement. There is no multi-prompt randomized trial, source-order reversal, semantic success rubric, or comparison with equal-cost switches selected by other transition diagnostics.

key_findings.claim: Appendix J asserts a six-prompt, equal-energy on-peak advantage without reporting the quantitative evidence needed to check that claim.
key_findings.evidence: Section J says on-peak perturbations produce systematically larger LPIPS than random off-peak perturbations and that the gap exceeds seed-to-seed variability across all six prompts. It provides no sample count, window-selection split, effect sizes, variability estimates, table, test statistic, confidence interval, or figure tied to this experiment. Representative images cannot verify the stated across-prompt quantitative comparison, so this result remains unsupported in the supplied manuscript.

anchors.section: J Stable Diffusion 3.5: CBD-peak intervention statistics

key_findings.claim: The advertised free-energy heatmaps are not an independent 'two-sided observable': the supplied figures construct the plotted energy proxy directly from TAD, making its agreement with TAD circular.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix K says F_sigma=-sigma^2 log p_sigma is estimated directly from the denoiser via Tweedie's formula, but gives no density-integration derivation or reference constant. Figures 35 and 36 explicitly label 'F proxy from TAD_actual' and display F(t)=-log(TAD/TAD_max); Figure 37 plots an axis called 'TAD ratio' against normalized trajectory index while labeling the surface F=-log p. Tweedie's identity yields a score/posterior-mean relation, not a scalar log density from one local evaluation; recovering log p requires integrating the score with a consistency path and normalization. A monotone transform of TAD must align with TAD by construction, so these panels cannot independently validate projection-caustic free-energy geometry.

anchors.section: Figure 37 TAD-ratio free-energy surface and Figure 38 proxies

method.core_idea: Model finite-noise denoising as Laplace competition among nearest-point branches of a smoothed data support, then detect rapid branch-responsibility changes through derivatives or finite differences of the normalized learned score direction and use those peaks to target interventions.
method.mechanism: Gaussian smoothing converts squared distance, support density, and curvature into a free energy. At an ordinary projection caustic, several local minima contribute a log-sum-exp and their softmax responsibilities switch across an O(sigma^2) band, sharply rotating the score. CBD measures the Jacobian norm of normalized direction; FD/TAD estimate it with perturbed denoiser calls; a pseudo-online ratio compares actual-time instability with low-noise reevaluation along a stored baseline trajectory. Perturbations or guidance are then applied in ranked windows.
assumptions: The data distribution is locally supported on finitely many smooth equal-dimensional branches with a smooth positive density.
Relevant nearest-point minima are nondegenerate and uniformly separated from all other support.
A unique nearest point is implicitly assumed to lie inside a sufficiently small tubular neighbourhood, excluding focal degeneracy even though main-text Theorem 2.1 does not say so.
The value-level Laplace remainder can be differentiated with uniform control to obtain the score remainder claimed in Corollary 2.4.
A learned denoiser's score is accurate enough for the exact-density caustic asymptotics to govern its finite-difference direction field.
Normalizing the score removes uninformative magnitude without amplifying numerical noise near small score norms.
Finite-difference probe scale proportional to noise is small enough for locality and large enough for numerical stability.
Reevaluating a stored state at a low-noise timestep yields a meaningful denominator even off that timestep's state distribution.
Windowed Gaussian perturbation effect on final L2 or LPIPS is a useful measure of branch sensitivity.
Per-run min-max and trajectory-length normalization preserve meaningful cross-model profile structure.
A high or inverted TAD score is consistently defined before it is used to rank sensitive windows.
The heatmap called free energy is an independently estimated density observable rather than the displayed monotone transform of TAD.
Toy nearest-support branch commitments are informative analogues of semantic commitments in learned diffusion models.

techniques.role: Expresses the exact score as a gradient of a temperature-like energy landscape.
Derives single-branch and multi-branch small-noise asymptotics.
Represents switching as log-sum-exp competition among nearest support branches.
Defines ideal CBD as local sensitivity of denoising direction.
Estimates Jacobian energy with perturbed denoiser evaluations.
Approximates directional instability along a baseline trajectory.
Normalizes trajectory instability by re-evaluating stored states at a late probe time.
Measures causal sensitivity by injecting equal-energy perturbations at candidate windows.
Applies classifier or branch control only in a detector-selected interval.
Produces figures labeled as free-energy diagnostics; the displayed implementation uses -log of normalized TAD and is therefore not independent.

evaluations.setting: Smooth projection-regular support and ordinary multi-branch caustic under exact Gaussian smoothing.
evaluations.metric: Uniform small-noise expansion of free energy and score.
evaluations.result: A nonfocal tubular branch gives squared-distance plus density/curvature corrections, and competing branches give a value-level log-sum-exp. Main Theorem 2.1 omits the tubular/nonfocal restriction, and the softmax score remainder is not proved by the appendix's differentiation of a uniform value error.
evaluations.baseline: Single nondegenerate nearest-point projection away from the cut/focal set.

evaluations.setting: Two-dimensional cusp and cross support simulations.
evaluations.metric: Commitment location, branch fraction, and intervention-step count relative to a CBD switching mask.
evaluations.result: Commitments are enriched in a mask covering 14.6% of the grid but only 47.1% occur inside; cross-band control reaches vertical fraction 0.8635 versus 0.5225 baseline while acting for 65.5/200 steps.
evaluations.baseline: No control and always-on control, the latter reaching 0.9640 vertical fraction.

evaluations.setting: One class-conditional MNIST DDPM baseline trajectory with future-count-selected prototype-repulsion windows.
evaluations.metric: Visual final-image change for windows 110-200, 250-350, 300-400, 50-75, and 85-110.
evaluations.result: The 110-200 and 50-75 interventions look more consequential than the displayed comparison windows, but the paper reports no numerical distance or semantic metric, repeat count, seed/class sweep, or matched random-window test.
evaluations.baseline: One unperturbed image and visually selected alternative time windows.

evaluations.setting: Five pretrained CIFAR-10 DDPM trajectories with sliding perturbation windows.
evaluations.metric: Per-trajectory Pearson correlation between normalized/inverted CBD proxy and final LPIPS.
evaluations.result: All five correlations exceed 0.84, with mean 0.928 and reported p<1e-70; raw-ratio correlations have the opposite sign by construction.
evaluations.baseline: Window position without the detector ranking.

evaluations.setting: CIFAR-10 DDPM pseudo-online re-noising on one seed-1000 trajectory and a second seed-42 width-15 sliding scan, with 24 trials per window.
evaluations.metric: Final pixel L2, per-pixel L1, LPIPS, and correlation with the displayed TAD ratio.
evaluations.result: Seed 1000 early [0,75] gives mean L2 43.32 and per-pixel L1 0.657 versus late [180,249] at 6.64 and 0.0756; the seed-42 earliest [0,14] gives L2 35.68/LPIPS 0.165 versus final [240,249] at 3.33/0.0053. Page 41 calls ratio correlations +0.913/+0.919, conflicting with the subsequent raw-ratio negative convention.
evaluations.baseline: Late and manually chosen windows on the same stored trajectories.

evaluations.setting: Cross-section audit of CIFAR Tables 3-4 and Figure 39.
evaluations.metric: Sign of association between raw normalized ratio R (or labeled CBD ratio) and downstream L2/LPIPS.
evaluations.result: Table 3 says raw R is negative (Pearson -0.6939/-0.7005; Spearman -0.9088/-0.8873) and 1-R positive, while Figure 39 says high-ratio groups (n=750 each) have larger effects; the labeling is not reconciled.
evaluations.baseline: Explicit raw-R versus inverted-1-R definitions in Table 3.

evaluations.setting: CIFAR-10 classifier guidance toward airplane over 250 reverse steps.
evaluations.metric: Target-class accuracy, LPIPS, guided steps, and runtime.
evaluations.result: Ten guided steps in fixed t=[30,70] reach 0.960 target accuracy, compared with 0.040 in fixed t=[180,220], approaching full 250-step guidance at much lower intervention count.
evaluations.baseline: Full classifier guidance, unguided sampling, and one late random/comparison band.

evaluations.setting: DiT, EDM2, SD3.5, CelebA-HQ DDPM, and an MDLM caveat under normalized TAD/free-energy profiles.
evaluations.metric: Qualitative peak, ridge, elbow, and plateau alignment after per-run normalization.
evaluations.result: Related multi-region shapes recur but shift by model and scheduler; no common raw threshold or timestep is established.
evaluations.baseline: Within-run time profile and model-specific intervention effects.

evaluations.setting: Thirty Stable Diffusion 3.5 prompt-seed runs with windowed latent perturbations.
evaluations.metric: Within-run Pearson and Spearman correlation of raw mean TAD ratio with final pixel L2 and LPIPS.
evaluations.result: Aggregated correlations are -0.470, -0.230, -0.887, and -0.577 respectively, indicating that lower raw TAD often ranks larger effects despite inconsistent high-TAD language elsewhere.
evaluations.baseline: All candidate windows within each same prompt-seed trajectory.

evaluations.setting: Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium fixed-prompt two-step scan versus the 30-run robustness study.
evaluations.metric: Window mean raw TAD ratio, final pixel L2, and LPIPS.
evaluations.result: For the single prompt, late (25,26) has TAD 0.503, L2 40.15, and LPIPS 0.196 versus early (0,1) at 0.051, 207.72, and 0.187, a 0.009 LPIPS edge without uncertainty. Across 30 runs the raw-ratio LPIPS relation is instead negative on average and highly variable (Pearson -0.230, std 0.430; one prompt is positive 0.620).
evaluations.baseline: Early, middle, and late equal-length windows, followed by six prompts times five seeds.

evaluations.setting: Stable Diffusion 3.5 prompt switching at a detector-profile elbow.
evaluations.metric: Qualitative retention or change of prompt semantics in eight generations.
evaluations.result: Outputs suggest different effects before and after the elbow, but the test uses one prompt pair and has no blinded quantitative success criterion.
evaluations.baseline: Switches at other trajectory phases shown qualitatively.

evaluations.setting: Appendix J claimed six-prompt on-peak versus random off-peak equal-energy intervention study.
evaluations.metric: Claimed LPIPS advantage relative to seed variability.
evaluations.result: No sample count, effect size, dispersion, table, test statistic, or dedicated figure is supplied, so the quantitative claim cannot be evaluated from the paper.
evaluations.baseline: Random off-peak windows as described in prose only.

evaluations.setting: DiT-XL/2, EDM2-XS, and SD3.5 panels presented as free-energy validation.
evaluations.metric: Independence and calibration of the plotted F_sigma=-sigma^2 log p_sigma estimate.
evaluations.result: Figures 35-36 label the quantity 'F proxy from TAD_actual' and plot -log(TAD/TAD_max); Figure 37 likewise uses a TAD-ratio axis. No score integration, density normalization, ground-truth calibration, or ridge-location error is reported, so TAD/free-energy agreement is circular.
evaluations.baseline: An independently reconstructed log density or known-density toy free energy, neither of which is provided for these panels.

limitations: Author-stated: CBD is not a universal order parameter or a direct zero-noise caustic estimator, and its band shifts with density, curvature, noise, and scheduler.
Author-stated: the theorem excludes focal and degenerate caustics that need different asymptotics.
Author-stated: the work is primarily a geometric theory and diagnostic study rather than a complete control algorithm.
Reviewer-identified: smooth finite-branch support assumptions are not validated for any learned image or latent distribution.
Reviewer-identified: main-text Theorem 2.1 omits the appendix's sufficiently-small-tubular-neighbourhood/nonfocal hypothesis, so unique projection alone does not justify the determinant expansion.
Reviewer-identified: Corollary 2.4 differentiates a uniform O(sigma^4) free-energy value remainder without a C1 remainder bound, leaving its stated O(1) score error unproved.
Reviewer-identified: score-model error is absent from the theory and not separated from true geometric instability empirically.
Reviewer-identified: pseudo-online CBD requires a completed baseline trajectory and off-time state reevaluation, so it is not an online trigger as deployed.
Reviewer-identified: raw TAD, normalized TAD, ratio, and inverted 1-TAD are named inconsistently; CIFAR page 41/Table 3/Figure 39 and the SD3.5 studies reverse the direction of effect.
Reviewer-identified: per-run min-max and trajectory normalization can make shapes visually comparable while discarding raw calibration.
Reviewer-identified: the cusp band misses 52.9% of commitments and depends on hand-chosen finite-noise and threshold choices.
Reviewer-identified: CIFAR guidance uses one fixed detector band and one late comparison band rather than prospective per-trajectory evaluation.

Reviewer-identified: the MNIST intervention is a single baseline trajectory judged from images, and prompt switching uses eight samples for one prompt pair; neither has a blinded quantitative semantic outcome.
Reviewer-identified: Appendix J's claimed six-prompt on-peak LPIPS advantage supplies no sample count, effect sizes, dispersion, table, or statistical test.

Reviewer-identified: the free-energy heatmaps are displayed as -log transforms of TAD_actual rather than an independently reconstructed log density, making their advertised two-sided agreement circular.
Reviewer-identified: finite-difference CBD adds denoiser calls and probe-scale choices, with little end-to-end overhead accounting beyond one guidance example.
failure_modes: Score normalization can explode direction noise where the score magnitude is near zero, creating a false CBD peak.
A learned denoiser error or scheduler discontinuity can rotate the update direction without any data-support caustic.
A true semantic branch transition can occur through a focal or high-order singularity excluded by the log-sum-exp theorem.
A focal point with a unique nearest projection can make I-A_nu singular and invalidate the main regular expansion despite satisfying the main text's stated uniqueness condition.
Differentiating a small uniform function-value error can yield an unbounded derivative, so an unproved score remainder can dominate the claimed branchwise mixture correction.
Off-time reevaluation can rank states by out-of-distribution denoiser behavior rather than future sensitivity.
Min-max normalization can promote a small numerical fluctuation to the apparent dominant critical band.
Using raw TAD in one experiment and 1-TAD in another can silently reverse the control policy.
Relabeling -log of normalized TAD as free energy creates guaranteed visual alignment and a false appearance of independent mechanistic confirmation.
A fixed average band can work on CIFAR while missing trajectory-specific commitments or merely exploiting a scheduler-wide sensitive phase.
Pixel L2 and LPIPS can disagree about which window matters, as seen in the SD3.5 early-versus-late scan.
Band-limited control can appear efficient while still occupying one third of a toy trajectory or being selected after inspecting effects.
Generated outputs can change substantially without switching semantic branch, or retain coarse semantics while changing the measured perceptual distance.
reusable_insights: Finite-noise density and curvature terms shift branch boundaries; zero-noise nearest-neighbor geometry alone is not a complete transition predictor.
Normalize vector direction when the scientific target is branching orientation, but always report the unnormalized score norm to diagnose numerical amplification.
Separate a detector's raw statistic, normalization, and inversion in names and plots so control direction cannot silently flip.
Evaluate critical-window detectors prospectively with equal-duration, equal-energy random and competing-diagnostic intervals on held-out trajectories.
Report enrichment and recall together: a small-area band containing 47.1% of commitments is informative but incomplete.
Use sliding-window interventions to test causal sensitivity rather than inferring it from a visually sharp diagnostic peak alone.
Quantify off-distribution error when reevaluating stored diffusion states at mismatched noise levels.
Treat theoretical normal forms as mechanism classes and explicitly audit data/model violations such as stratification, degeneracy, and score error.
Before differentiating an asymptotic expansion, prove a parameter-uniform derivative remainder or differentiate the defining integral directly.
Validate a score-derived free energy by path-consistent score integration and an independent reference, never by a monotone transform of the detector being validated.
open_questions: Can an actually online, one-pass CBD estimator predict a sensitive interval before intervening, without a stored baseline trajectory or low-noise reevaluation?
What fixed sign convention best unifies raw CBD, TAD ratio, and inverted profiles across CIFAR and SD3.5?
Do CBD rankings beat simple timestep, score-norm, SNR, Jacobian-norm, attention-change, or nonlocality baselines on held-out prompts?
How sensitive are peaks and intervention results to finite-difference direction, probe count, delta, smoothing, and min-max normalization?
Can known synthetic densities quantify caustic-location error, recall, precision, and free-energy reconstruction bias?
How do focal, cusp, stratified, unequal-dimensional, or discrete data supports change the detector's predicted signature?
Can score-estimation error be included in the asymptotics and separated empirically from geometric branch competition?
Can Corollary 2.4 be repaired with a uniform C1 Laplace expansion, and what score error rate follows under explicit branch regularity?
Can log density be reconstructed path-independently from the denoiser score and calibrated against a known-density model, rather than proxied by TAD?
Does a detector-selected window remain causally superior under pre-registered per-trajectory selection and many matched random bands?
Which outcome defines semantic commitment most reliably across images, latent text-to-image models, audio, video, and discrete diffusion?
Can CBD guide adaptive compute or conditioning while reducing total denoiser calls after accounting for the probes needed to estimate it?

competitive_landscape.title: The Geometry of Phase Transitions in Diffusion Models: Tubular Neighbourhoods and Singularities
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct same-line predecessor connecting diffusion phase transitions to injectivity radius, tubular neighborhoods, and projection singularities.
competitive_landscape.difference: Yaguchi et al. develop the single-valued projection/tubular-neighborhood picture and empirical singularity diagnostics. The present paper extends that geometry to explicit finite-noise multi-branch log-sum-exp competition and introduces CBD/TAD interventions, while inheriting the need to validate manifold and score assumptions in learned models.

competitive_landscape.title: A Phase Transition in Diffusion Models Reveals the Hierarchical Nature of Data
competitive_landscape.relationship: Primary theoretical and empirical account of class-level phase transitions in hierarchical diffusion data.
competitive_landscape.difference: Sclocchi et al. derive a population transition where high-level class reconstruction changes sharply while low-level details evolve smoothly, and test ImageNet models. The present work supplies a local trajectory geometry and intervention diagnostic, but does not directly compare CBD against the hierarchical transition prediction.

competitive_landscape.title: Dynamical Regimes of Diffusion Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: Foundational statistical-physics account of speciation and collapse transitions during reverse diffusion.
competitive_landscape.difference: Biroli et al. characterize population-level speciation from covariance spectra and later collapse toward memorized samples in high-dimensional limits. The present paper instead targets local nearest-branch competition along individual trajectories; a head-to-head test could determine whether CBD adds information beyond predicted speciation time.

competitive_landscape.title: Concurrence of Symmetry Breaking and Nonlocality Phase Transitions in Diffusion Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: Contemporary empirical study of critical windows in modern diffusion Transformers using symmetry-breaking and nonlocality diagnostics.
competitive_landscape.difference: Zhang et al. compare two operational phase-transition notions and report near-concurrent critical times in modern DiTs. The present paper proposes projection-caustic geometry and score-direction instability as a mechanism and control signal, but does not benchmark CBD against those two direct diagnostics on the same trajectories.

competitive_landscape.title: Manifolds, Random Matrices and Spectral Gaps: The geometric phases of generative diffusion
competitive_landscape.relationship: Closest score-geometry phase analysis using Jacobian spectra under the manifold hypothesis.
competitive_landscape.difference: Ventura et al. derive score-Jacobian spectral gaps and three phases—trivial, manifold coverage, and consolidation—and compare them with trained networks. The target instead studies local nearest-projection branch competition and normalized direction instability, but it does not benchmark CBD against the spectral-gap diagnostic or establish that its peaks identify a distinct transition.

competitive_landscape.title: The statistical thermodynamics of generative diffusion models: Phase transitions, symmetry breaking and critical instability
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct free-energy and critical-instability predecessor for diffusion dynamics.
competitive_landscape.difference: Ambrogioni formulates reverse diffusion as a stochastic adiabatic process minimizing free energy and derives mean-field symmetry-breaking transitions and critical exponents. The target adds projection-caustic branch geometry and an intervention heuristic, but its learned-model free-energy panels are TAD transforms rather than an independent thermodynamic measurement.

competitive_landscape.title: How Out-of-Equilibrium Phase Transitions can Seed Pattern Formation in Trained Diffusion Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: Contemporary theory-plus-intervention competitor identifying critical times in trained diffusion models.
competitive_landscape.difference: Ambrogioni predicts criticality through softening Fourier modes and growing spatial correlation length, validates those signatures in convolutional and ImageNet diffusion models, and applies guidance pulses at the estimated critical time. The target proposes nearest-branch caustics and score-direction finite differences instead, but supplies no same-trajectory comparison against correlation-length or mode-softening diagnostics.

competitive_landscape.title: Applying Guidance in a Limited Interval Improves Sample and Distribution Quality in Diffusion Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct predecessor for temporally restricted diffusion guidance and intervention efficiency.
competitive_landscape.difference: Kynkäänniemi et al. systematically show that guidance is harmful early, useful in a middle interval, and unnecessary late across architectures and datasets, improving ImageNet-512 FID from 1.81 to 1.40. The target tries to choose windows from a geometric diagnostic, but its CIFAR study compares only one fixed detector band with one late band and does not benchmark against this established limited-guidance schedule.

competitive_landscape.title: Spontaneous Symmetry Breaking in Generative Diffusion Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: Foundational phase-transition and critical-window account with a sampling intervention.
competitive_landscape.difference: Raya and Ambrogioni locate a stability-breaking transition from a central fixed point to data-manifold attraction and exploit it through Gaussian late initialization, reporting up to threefold FID improvements for fast samplers. The target uses local projection-branch competition and CBD/TAD rather than central stability, yet does not show that CBD outpredicts the earlier transition time or sampling intervention.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims a unified geometric mechanism for generative phase transitions—finite-noise softmax competition near projection caustics—and a model-agnostic Critical Boundary Detector that localizes causally sensitive windows.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The clearest technical contribution is a finite-noise, value-level multi-branch Laplace/log-sum-exp normal form for ordinary smooth projection competition, extending the authors' earlier tubular-neighbourhood account. The paper then couples normalized-score finite differences to toy branch control, CIFAR perturbation correlations and restricted guidance, cross-model profiles, and small SD3.5 interventions. The strongest empirical evidence is the reproducible magnitude of CIFAR window-ranking correlations after an explicitly chosen inversion, not the free-energy panels.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: Narrow novelty: an ordinary nondegenerate projection-caustic value expansion plus a broad exploratory TAD intervention heuristic. The regular theorem needs the appendix's unstated nonfocal tubular restriction, and the score corollary lacks derivative-remainder control. Prior work already provides tubular projection geometry, symmetry-breaking/free-energy theories, spectral and correlation-length critical diagnostics, and limited-interval guidance. Learned-support assumptions remain untested; pseudo-online evaluation is retrospective and off-time; ratio signs conflict across tables/figures; Appendix J omits its claimed statistics; and the 'independent' free-energy plots are monotone transforms of TAD. CBD is therefore not yet validated as a caustic detector or universal phase marker.

reviewer_notes: Secondary verification independently reread all 54 pages of the exact pinned PDF, including full proofs B-C, numerical appendices D-M, every table, and all figure-only panels. OCR-ambiguous/image-dominant pages 38 and 50 and the decisive free-energy/sign panels on pages 52-54 were inspected directly from rendered PDF pages. The pass rechecked all 18 findings and 13 evaluations, correcting the regular-theorem scope, the unproved differentiation of the value remainder, the unsupported Appendix-J result, the ratio-sign contradictions, and the circular TAD-derived free-energy claim. Nine closest primary competitors were re-searched and pinned to current official arXiv/OpenReview versions on 2026-08-23. Residual uncertainty is whether the score corollary can be repaired under stronger C1 hypotheses and whether some plotted labels reflect undocumented code transformations; neither is resolved by the manuscript.
